title: 'He didn't deserve to die like this'; Son shot dead by police in park on the weekend He was 'going through a rough time,' mother says: [ONT Edition]
article: Earle Reid and two of his children were just returning home after visiting a neighbour Sunday afternoon when he noticed a car and two men in front of his house.

The men identified themselves as investigators with the provincial Special Investigations Unit. They told him that his eldest child O'brien Christopher\-Reid had been shot dead by police earlier in the day, near a footpath in Wilket Creek Park.

Reid couldn't believe what he was hearing. His youngest son, Daniel, fell to the ground sobbing. Reid did his best to comfort him and his teenage daughter, then called his ex-wife Jacqueline Christopher. She was devastated.
Their burning question How could this happen? Nobody seems to have an answer.
Neither Reid nor Christopher had spoken to their eldest son that weekend. What's more, they had no idea why he was even in Wilket Creek Park.
After meeting with SIU investigators yesterday Christopher- Reid's parents remain perplexed.
"All they (the SIU) told us is that he died from gunshot wounds," said Reid during an interview with the Star.
"I'm just trusting, having faith in God and faith in the SIU that they're doing everything to the best of their abilities."
But his voice cracked as he spoke of his son.
"He was a human being. He didn't deserve to die like this."

Now the parents are calling on anybody who witnessed the events in the park to come forward and talk to the SIU, a provincial body called in whenever someone is killed or seriously injured and police are involved.

The events of last Sunday began to unfold around noon, when police were called after there were reports of an emotionally disturbed young man carrying a knife along Lawrence Ave. E., heading for Edwards Gardens.
Three officers searched for the man, and according to sources and witnesses, caught up with him in Wilket Creek Park, which is connected to Edwards Gardens. They tried to calm him down.
But according to sources, the man started to run. The officers followed and, when they caught up to him, he lunged at them with a knife. All three officers then fired their guns, sources said.
Christopher said her son was "going through a rough time" and had some emotional issues.
"He felt he could do more, that he had more to offer," she explained as she choked back her words and bowed her head.
But, based on the advice of her lawyer Steven Skurka, she wouldn't comment on suggestions that her son had any history of mental illness.

"Even if he was emotionally disturbed, why did they have to shoot him?" she asked. "They're (the police) there to protect everybody. ... What crime was he committing? Who was he threatening? Did he steal anything from anyone? Why did this happen?"
Ironically his mother was at a police picnic on Saturday in the Malvern community where she lives. The purpose to honour the Agincourt Church of God for its work in the community.
She and Reid paint a picture of a bright 26-year-old man who was trying to find his way in the world.
Christopher-Reid had studied chemical engineering at Ryerson University. He did well at school, they said.

But after two years, he decided to take a year off, and got a job working at American Express. He had moved out to Vancouver for a while, but moved back last July. He loved basketball, politics and rap music, his father said. Christopher had spoken to her son just a couple of weeks ago, and he had recently left a message for her.
"He told me he loved me and he would be in touch."
